docs.text: Data Analytics ¶ Learn to turn a business question into a recommendation you can defend, using Tableau and real analytical habits. Welcome! I'm Aayush, your facilitator for this training programme. We will use Tableau to explore and explain data from five areas of a business: retail and e-commerce, finance, operations, marketing and HR. Along the way you will also practise on sports, technology, government and other datasets. This site is still being built Right now you will find the course foundation and the proposed roadmap. Full lessons, datasets, workbooks and Python companions are on their way. The business cases and the lesson template are previews. They are not ready-to-run assignments yet. Course at a glance ¶ Twelve live classes. Two hours each, spread across several weeks, plus independent practice between classes. Spreadsheet basics are enough. No Python or Tableau experience is assumed. We start from the beginning. Tableau Public. You will work with synthetic and public datasets only, never private workplace data. Portfolio and briefing. You finish with a practical portfolio and an executive briefing grounded in checked evidence. Where to start ¶ Work through these pages in order before the first class: Learning roadmap : what each of the twelve classes covers. Setup and practice : what you need installed and how to keep notes. Analytical workflow : the seven steps we use in every analysis. Business cases : the five business problems you will solve. How we will practise ¶ Every topic follows the same rhythm: Watch a short demonstration. Follow a guided exercise together. Solve a related problem on your own. Debug a deliberate mistake. Recommend an action to a stakeholder. One habit to build from day one Before you trust a chart, check three things: what each row means, how the metric is defined, and what evidence supports the number. Python is optional at first. Every essential Tableau task can be done without writing code. Instructor solutions are shared separately after each practice round. Connect with Aayush on LinkedIn

docs.text: Business case previews ¶ Five business problems, one for each department. Each case teaches a core skill and a common mistake to catch. Previews, not assignments yet These are proposed case themes. Individual files have not been released for class. We combine selected Tableau sample datasets with synthetic (made-up) teaching data. Meridian Commerce is a proposed fictional company used only for the synthetic cases. Real datasets keep their own context, units and dates. The five core cases ¶ Retail ¶ Decision: Which customer segment deserves a closer investigation? You will practise: what a row means, distinct orders, average order value, Sales and Profit, ratios, discounts, customers, trends and the limits of a returns list. Mistake to catch: treating order lines as orders. Finance ¶ Decision: Which departments need a spending review? You will practise: budget versus actual, time periods, reconciliation and whether a cost difference is favourable. Mistake to catch: repeating a monthly budget on every transaction row. Operations ¶ Decision: Where should delivery reliability improve? You will practise: promised dates, overdue open shipments, distributions, median and mean. Mistake to catch: dropping undelivered shipments from the service measure. Marketing ¶ Decision: Which campaigns need closer evaluation before budget moves? You will practise: weighted funnel rates, cost per conversion, return on ad spend and the limits of attribution. Mistake to catch: averaging percentages that have different denominators. HR ¶ Decision: How is the workforce changing, and which comparisons are fair? You will practise: historical headcount, turnover, cohorts, tenure and recruitment timelines. All employee records are synthetic. Mistake to catch: dividing past exits by the current headcount. What every case includes ¶ Stakeholder brief : the decision and why it matters Data dictionary : what each field means Metric definitions : exact formulas and scope Worked example : a guided walk-through Exercises : guided and independent practice Debugging task : find and fix a mistake Recommendation challenge : advise the stakeholder Validation checkpoints : confirm your numbers Each case also has an optional pandas connection. Instructor answers are supplied separately. Combining evidence across departments ¶ Before combining findings, explain any differences in grain, period and units. Within the synthetic company, marketing-attributed revenue is a view of the same retail revenue. Do not count it twice. Separate catalog datasets do not describe that fictional company. A good recommendation weighs trade-offs. It does not add incompatible KPIs together. Additional practice choices ¶ You will also be able to practise on topics beyond the five departments: Topic Example dataset Sports World Cup match results Technology Mobile operating-system usage (a data-quality exercise), start-up funding Government US construction spending, US home sales Other Science, education and entertainment datasets These are transfer exercises: the same process, with source-specific definitions and checks. They fit into your existing practice time or optional extensions. The five core cases remain the foundation of your portfolio. Every dataset is reviewed first A dataset appearing in a catalog does not tell us what each row means, which calculations it supports or whether it can be shared. Each lesson will give you the exact reviewed file and dictionary, or instructions to download it from the source, before you use it.

docs.text: Learning roadmap ¶ Twelve two-hour classes, grouped into three stages. Each class starts from a business question and ends with a piece of evidence for your portfolio. This is a proposed sequence Lesson instructions and data are released only after they have been checked. Class dates and the final workload will be confirmed separately. Stage 1: Foundations with retail data ¶ Classes 1 to 4. You learn Tableau and the core habits of careful analysis using one retail dataset. Class Business question You will produce 1 What makes a business question answerable? Tableau orientation and your first chart. A question, its population and a first evidence view. 2 What does a retail row represent? Data types, keys and preparation. A grain statement and a quality checklist. 3 Which retail segment deserves a closer look? Distinct orders, Sales, Profit, average order value and profit ratio. A checked KPI worksheet and a short debugging explanation. 4 How do trends and returns change the decision? Monthly growth and dashboard design. A retail dashboard and a recommendation. Stage 2: One department at a time ¶ Classes 5 to 8. Each class is a new business area. Support is gradually reduced so you work more independently. Class Business question You will produce 5 Finance: where is spending above plan? A reconciled budget-versus-actual view. 6 Operations: where do deliveries miss their promise? A service view that includes still-pending shipments. 7 Marketing: which campaigns need a closer look? A campaign comparison with notes on denominators. 8 HR: how is the workforce changing? A synthetic workforce snapshot and a fair comparison. Stage 3: Bring it together ¶ Classes 9 to 12. You combine evidence from several departments into one executive recommendation. Class Business question You will produce 9 Which departmental findings agree or conflict? A five-domain evidence register and a briefing proposal. 10 What decision should executives make? A draft briefing with traceable evidence. 11 Does the recommendation survive scrutiny? A validation log and a revised briefing. 12 What action and follow-up measure should leaders approve? The final executive briefing and a portfolio reflection. What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of the course you should be able to: Turn a stakeholder's concern into a clear question with a population, a period and a decision. Identify what a row means, the keys, data types, units and missing records, and document your preparation. Calculate metrics with the right aggregation and the right denominator. Check results with reconciliations, small manual checks and alternative explanations. Build readable Tableau views and dashboards that make the important comparison obvious. Recommend an action while explaining limitations, trade-offs and how success will be measured. Practice time ¶ How much time to plan outside class The recommended essential route is about 19 hours of practice in total: 60 to 90 minutes in most weeks about 2 hours in project weeks Optional deeper practice brings this to about 25 hours . Both figures are estimates that will be tested in a pilot before the schedule is fixed. How you will be assessed ¶ Your portfolio includes evidence from all five business areas. Your final briefing combines findings from at least three of them. The exact submission schedule and presentation format will be shared before assessment begins. Feedback rewards correct reasoning and careful checking, not only attractive charts. Extra practice topics ¶ Alongside the five business areas, selected datasets from the Tableau sample-data catalog give you choices in sports, technology, government and more. These use the same question-to-recommendation workflow and fit into your existing practice time or optional extensions. Each dataset keeps its own real dates, units and context.

docs.text: Setup and practice ¶ What you need before the first class, how to stay safe with data, and how to keep a simple evidence log. What you need ¶ A computer that can run Tableau Public Permission to install software on it A way to receive course files and submit your work Before teaching starts We will confirm operating systems, installation permissions, accessibility needs and the submission channel with everyone. No course data files are available yet. Install Tableau Desktop Public Edition ¶ This is the version we use for all class instructions. Open the official Tableau Public page . Check that your computer meets the listed requirements. Download and install Tableau Desktop Public Edition . Before class, you will receive a small synthetic CSV file and a short smoke test. It asks you to: Open the CSV in Tableau. Check the data types of the fields. Create a simple sum. Save the workbook on your computer. Close it and open it again. Exact menu steps will be added once they have been rehearsed on the course version of Tableau. Keep your data safe ¶ Anything you publish to Tableau Public is public Published workbooks and their data can be seen by anyone. Hiding an item on your profile does not make it private, because it can still be reached through its link. Use only the datasets supplied for this course. Never upload private employer, customer or employee files. Tableau Public lets you save workbooks on your own computer . Submitting a local workbook is an accepted course route, so publishing online is optional. You can read more in Tableau's Public FAQ and saving guide . If something does not work ¶ Installation or internet trouble Follow the demonstration or pair with a classmate, and keep writing your metric and checking notes. Complete your own workbook later, once access is back. A browser-only version of Tableau may look different from the desktop instructions. It will only replace the desktop route once it has its own tested instructions. Optional Python path ¶ You do not need Python for the essential lessons. Later, optional companions will show how the same Tableau ideas (selecting rows, grouping, distinct counts and date rules) look in pandas. Installation instructions will come with those notebooks once they are tested. Keep an evidence log ¶ For every task, write down a few short notes. They make your portfolio much easier to build. Record Example prompt Data release Which file and version did I use? Question What decision is this for? Grain What does one row represent? Date window and filters Which records are included? Metric definition What is the numerator and denominator? Checks How did I confirm the number is right? Chart and recommendation What should the stakeholder do next? Save your workbook and your notes together. When two numbers disagree Compare their populations and denominators before changing the chart.

docs.text: From business question to recommendation ¶ A useful analysis supports a decision. A chart becomes trustworthy when its population, calculations and limitations are clear. We follow the same seven steps in every class. The seven steps ¶ 1. Business question ¶ Ask: Who must decide what, and by when? Keep: the decision and a one-sentence question. 2. Data understanding ¶ Ask: What does each row represent? What is missing? Keep: the grain, keys, units, data dictionary and scope. 3. Preparation ¶ Ask: What changes are needed, and could someone else repeat them? Keep: an untouched copy of the original data and a log of every change. 4. Analysis ¶ Ask: Which comparison or metric actually answers the question? Keep: the metric definition, filters and calculation. 5. Validation ¶ Ask: Do totals reconcile? Can I explain any odd values? Keep: a manual spot check, count and total checks, and edge cases. 6. Visualization ¶ Ask: Can the audience see the important comparison at a glance? Keep: a labelled chart showing the period, units and population. 7. Recommendation ¶ Ask: What action follows, and what is still uncertain? Keep: an action linked to evidence, one caveat and a follow-up measure. A worked example ¶ Why are orders falling? A manager asks: "Why are orders falling?" The data file has one row per order line , so a single order with three products takes up three rows. Counting rows would count lines , not orders. First, define what an order is, which period to look at and which orders are eligible. Then count distinct order IDs in that population. Compare the result with an order-level summary before reading anything into the trend. The same care applies elsewhere in the course: a budget repeated on every row after a join undelivered shipments left out of a service calculation campaign percentages averaged without their volumes past staff exits divided by today's headcount When a result looks wrong ¶ Work through these checks in order: Grain and keys Date filters Missing values Join or relationship behaviour Aggregation Then write down why the wrong answer was tempting and what evidence supports the corrected one. A plausible number is not a checked number Looking reasonable is not the same as being validated. Association is not causation ¶ A pattern in the data can tell you where to look . It does not prove that a discount, campaign, carrier or HR policy caused a result. When a decision depends on cause and effect, recommend a follow-up comparison or a test.

docs.text: Class 1: From decision to evidence ¶ Turn a vague business request into a clear question, open your first dataset in Tableau, and build a first chart you can explain. Draft lesson The Tableau steps on this page have not yet been rehearsed on the course version of Tableau. Menu names may differ slightly on your computer. Your facilitator will confirm them in class. The business decision ¶ The head of a retail business says: "Sales feel uneven across our customer groups. I need to know where to look first." This is not yet a question you can answer with data. Today you will turn it into one, and then take a first look at the evidence. About the data We use a fictitious retail sample published by Tableau (the "Superstore" sample), prepared for this course. It is not a real company. Sales and Profit are in the file's own monetary units; the currency is not stated, so we never label it as dollars, rupees or anything else. What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of this class you will be able to: Write a business question that names a decision, a population and a time period. Connect Tableau to a CSV file and recognise dimensions and measures. Build a simple bar chart and add a filter. Explain the difference between one row and one order in this file. Save your workbook on your computer and reopen it. Evidence you keep: your written question, a saved first chart and a one-sentence explanation of what a row means. Before class ¶ Install Tableau Desktop Public Edition (see Setup and practice ). Complete the smoke test: open a CSV, create a sum, save, close and reopen. Get the course file order_lines.csv (release superstore-retail-v1 ) from your facilitator. Save it in a folder you can find again, for example Documents/DataAnalytics/data . If Tableau will not install or open Tell your facilitator before class. You can follow the demonstration, pair with a classmate and still write your question and notes. You will build your own chart later. Part 1: From request to question ¶ A good analytical question answers four things: Part Ask yourself Example Decision What will someone do differently? Choose one customer segment to investigate next month Population Which records count? All order lines in the course file Period Which dates? Orders placed in 2023, 2024 and 2025 Measure What will we compare? Sales by customer segment Putting it together: "Which customer segment had the highest Sales for orders placed in 2023–2025, so we can choose one segment to investigate next month?" Your turn (5 minutes) Rewrite the head's request as your own question. Use the four parts in the table. Keep it to one sentence. Part 2: Watch the demonstration ¶ Your facilitator will connect to the file and build a first chart while you watch. Before each step, predict what you think will happen. Things to notice: How Tableau reads each column (text, number or date). Which fields appear as dimensions (things you group by) and which as measures (numbers you add up). What happens to a number when you drag it into the view. Part 3: Guided practice ¶ Follow along step by step. Connect to the file ¶ Open Tableau Desktop Public Edition. In the Connect pane on the left, under To a File , choose Text file . Find and open order_lines.csv . Tableau opens the Data Source page with a preview of the rows. Check the column types ¶ Look at the small icon above each column in the preview: Icon Meaning Examples in this file Abc Text order_id, segment, region # Number sales, profit, quantity Calendar Date order_date, ship_date Check the IDs order_id and row_id are identifiers, not amounts. Adding them up means nothing. If an ID shows as a number, note it in your log. Tableau may tidy column names for display, for example showing order_id as Order Id . It is the same field. Build a first chart ¶ Click the Sheet 1 tab at the bottom. In the Data pane, find Segment and drag it to Rows . Find Sales and drag it to Columns . You should see one bar per segment. Tableau shows this as SUM(Sales) . Add a filter ¶ Drag Region to the Filters card. Tick one region and click OK . Watch how the bars change. Then clear the filter so all regions are included again. Write it down Every time you filter, record it. A chart without its filters written down is easy to misread later. Save and reopen ¶ Choose File → Save As and save the workbook in your course folder, for example class01_first_view . Close Tableau, open it again and open your saved workbook. Check that the chart and your filter settings are still there. Part 4: Rows versus orders ¶ Open the Data Source page again and look at a few rows that share the same order_id . One row in this file is one order line : one product within an order. One order can have several lines. So the number of rows is not the number of orders. Quick check In the Data pane, Tableau lists a field named after the file with (Count) at the end. Drag it to the view. Is that counting rows or orders? Write your answer in one sentence. You will measure orders properly in Class 2. Part 5: Independent work ¶ On a new sheet, build one more simple view on your own: Choose a different grouping: Region or Category . Show Sales for each group. Add a title that says what the chart shows and for which period. Write one sentence describing what the chart shows. Do not explain why yet. Part 6: Challenge ¶ A colleague says: "The biggest bar is the best segment, so we should invest there." In two or three sentences, explain why a bigger Sales bar alone does not tell us where to invest. What else would you want to see? Exit ticket ¶ Before you leave, write: Your one-sentence business question. What one row in order_lines.csv represents. One thing you are still unsure about. After class (about 1 hour) ¶ Fix anything that did not work during setup. Read the Analytical workflow page. Start your evidence log (see Setup and practice ) with today's question, file name and filters.

docs.text: By the end of this class you will be able to: Write a business question that names a decision, a population and a time period. Connect Tableau to a CSV file and recognise dimensions and measures. Build a simple bar chart and add a filter. Explain the difference between one row and one order in this file. Save your workbook on your computer and reopen it. Evidence you keep: your written question, a saved first chart and a one-sentence explanation of what a row means.
docs.title: What you will be able to do

docs.text: Install Tableau Desktop Public Edition (see Setup and practice ). Complete the smoke test: open a CSV, create a sum, save, close and reopen. Get the course file order_lines.csv (release superstore-retail-v1 ) from your facilitator. Save it in a folder you can find again, for example Documents/DataAnalytics/data . If Tableau will not install or open Tell your facilitator before class. You can follow the demonstration, pair with a classmate and still write your question and notes. You will build your own chart later.
docs.title: Before class

docs.text: A good analytical question answers four things: Part Ask yourself Example Decision What will someone do differently? Choose one customer segment to investigate next month Population Which records count? All order lines in the course file Period Which dates? Orders placed in 2023, 2024 and 2025 Measure What will we compare? Sales by customer segment Putting it together: "Which customer segment had the highest Sales for orders placed in 2023–2025, so we can choose one segment to investigate next month?" Your turn (5 minutes) Rewrite the head's request as your own question. Use the four parts in the table. Keep it to one sentence.
docs.title: Part 1: From request to question

docs.text: Your facilitator will connect to the file and build a first chart while you watch. Before each step, predict what you think will happen. Things to notice: How Tableau reads each column (text, number or date). Which fields appear as dimensions (things you group by) and which as measures (numbers you add up). What happens to a number when you drag it into the view.
docs.title: Part 2: Watch the demonstration

docs.text: Follow along step by step.
docs.title: Part 3: Guided practice

docs.text: Open Tableau Desktop Public Edition. In the Connect pane on the left, under To a File , choose Text file . Find and open order_lines.csv . Tableau opens the Data Source page with a preview of the rows.
docs.title: Connect to the file

docs.text: Look at the small icon above each column in the preview: Icon Meaning Examples in this file Abc Text order_id, segment, region # Number sales, profit, quantity Calendar Date order_date, ship_date Check the IDs order_id and row_id are identifiers, not amounts. Adding them up means nothing. If an ID shows as a number, note it in your log. Tableau may tidy column names for display, for example showing order_id as Order Id . It is the same field.
docs.title: Check the column types

docs.text: Click the Sheet 1 tab at the bottom. In the Data pane, find Segment and drag it to Rows . Find Sales and drag it to Columns . You should see one bar per segment. Tableau shows this as SUM(Sales) .
docs.title: Build a first chart

docs.text: Drag Region to the Filters card. Tick one region and click OK . Watch how the bars change. Then clear the filter so all regions are included again. Write it down Every time you filter, record it. A chart without its filters written down is easy to misread later.
docs.title: Add a filter

docs.text: Choose File → Save As and save the workbook in your course folder, for example class01_first_view . Close Tableau, open it again and open your saved workbook. Check that the chart and your filter settings are still there.
docs.title: Save and reopen

docs.text: Open the Data Source page again and look at a few rows that share the same order_id . One row in this file is one order line : one product within an order. One order can have several lines. So the number of rows is not the number of orders. Quick check In the Data pane, Tableau lists a field named after the file with (Count) at the end. Drag it to the view. Is that counting rows or orders? Write your answer in one sentence. You will measure orders properly in Class 2.
docs.title: Part 4: Rows versus orders

docs.text: On a new sheet, build one more simple view on your own: Choose a different grouping: Region or Category . Show Sales for each group. Add a title that says what the chart shows and for which period. Write one sentence describing what the chart shows. Do not explain why yet.
docs.title: Part 5: Independent work

docs.text: A colleague says: "The biggest bar is the best segment, so we should invest there." In two or three sentences, explain why a bigger Sales bar alone does not tell us where to invest. What else would you want to see?
docs.title: Part 6: Challenge

docs.text: Before you leave, write: Your one-sentence business question. What one row in order_lines.csv represents. One thing you are still unsure about.
docs.title: Exit ticket

docs.text: Fix anything that did not work during setup. Read the Analytical workflow page. Start your evidence log (see Setup and practice ) with today's question, file name and filters.
docs.title: After class (about 1 hour)

docs.text: Class 2: Can we trust the sales table? ¶ Before comparing anything, find out exactly what the retail file contains: what a row is, which columns can be added up, and how to count orders correctly. Draft lesson The Tableau steps on this page have not yet been rehearsed on the course version of Tableau. Menu names may differ slightly on your computer. The business decision ¶ The retail head now asks: "Before you show me any chart, can I trust these numbers? How many orders did we actually have?" A wrong count at this stage spoils every later chart. Today is about building trust in the data. What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of this class you will be able to: State the grain of the file: what one row represents. Tell which columns are identifiers, categories, dates or amounts. Count orders correctly with a distinct count. Explain what the returns flag does and does not tell you. Check a small slice of data by hand. Record what you changed in a short preparation log . Evidence you keep: a grain statement, a short quality checklist, a preparation log and one checked order. Before class ¶ Bring your saved Class 1 workbook and your evidence log. Keep the original order_lines.csv untouched. If you ever need to experiment, work on a copy. Part 1: Meet the data dictionary ¶ Every column has a job. Knowing that job tells you how to use it. Column What it is Can you add it up? row_id Unique number for each order line No, it is an identifier order_id Order identifier; repeats across that order's lines No, count it distinctly order_date , ship_date Calendar dates No order_month First day of the order's month, for monthly grouping No ship_mode Shipping service chosen No customer_id Fictitious customer identifier No segment Customer group: Consumer, Corporate or Home Office No, use it to group country_region , region Location labels No, use them to group category , sub_category Product groups No, use them to group product_id , product_name Product identifier and name No sales Sales reported for the line, in the file's own monetary units Yes quantity Number of items on the line Yes , but it counts items, not orders profit Profit reported for the line (can be negative) Yes discount Discount value as given in the source No, its exact definition is not documented returned_order_flag 1 if the order appears on the source's returns list, otherwise 0 Not on line rows (see Part 4) order_to_ship_days Days between order date and ship date No, not without care customer_analysis_eligible , customer_order_conflict Flags for a small data issue with customer IDs Used only for customer analysis later Scope of this file The file contains orders placed from 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2025 . A few orders placed late in 2025 shipped in early 2026; they are kept because the order date is what defines the period. Part 2: Find the grain ¶ Grain means: what does one row represent? Open your workbook and go to the Data Source page. Sort or scan the preview by order_id . Find an order that appears on more than one row . Compare those rows. What is the same? What is different? Write your grain statement Complete this sentence in your log: "One row in order_lines.csv represents one _ _ , identified by ____ ." Part 3: Count orders correctly ¶ Demonstration ¶ Your facilitator will show two numbers side by side: the number of rows (the field ending in (Count) ) the number of distinct orders Predict before you see them: will the two numbers be equal, or which will be larger? Guided practice ¶ On a new sheet, drag the (Count) field to the view. This counts rows. Drag Order Id into the view as well. Right-click it and choose Measure → Count (Distinct) . This counts orders. Put both numbers in a small table and label them clearly. Write one sentence explaining why they differ. A reusable calculation You can also create a calculated field named Orders with the formula: COUNTD([Order Id]) Use this whenever a chart needs a number of orders. Part 4: What the returns flag means ¶ returned_order_flag is 1 when an order appears on the source's returns list . Be careful with what it does not tell you: It has no return date, quantity or refund amount. A 0 means not on the list . It does not prove the order was never returned. The flag repeats on every line of a listed order. A common mistake Adding up returned_order_flag across lines counts lines of returned orders, not returned orders . To count returned orders, count distinct order_id values where the flag is 1. Part 5: Check one order by hand ¶ Pick one order with several lines. Filter the view to that single order_id . Show each line's sales and profit in a table. Add up the lines yourself on paper or in a spreadsheet. Compare with Tableau's total for that order. Do they match? Record the order ID, your hand total and Tableau's total in your log. Part 6: Keep a preparation log ¶ Write down every change you make to how the data is read or shaped, even small ones. Date What I changed Why How I checked it example Created calculated field Orders = COUNTD([Order Id]) Rows are order lines, not orders Compared with the row count; checked one order by hand The original file is never edited. Every change lives in Tableau or in your log. Part 7: Independent work ¶ For each Segment , build a small table showing: the number of rows, the number of distinct orders, total sales . Then answer in your log: Do the segment order counts add up to the overall order count? Why might that be true for Segment? Try the same with Category . Do category order counts add up to the overall total? Why not? Think about it Can one order contain products from more than one category? Can one order belong to more than one segment? Part 8: Debugging challenge ¶ A colleague sends this summary: "We had [row count] orders, and [sum of returned_order_flag] of them were returned." Which two mistakes are in this sentence? What should each number be counting instead? How would you check your corrected numbers? Write your corrected sentence. You do not need to share the numbers with anyone yet. Exit ticket ¶ Your grain statement. Why rows and orders differ in this file. One thing the returns flag cannot tell you. After class (about 1.5 hours) ¶ Finish the Segment and Category tables from Part 7. Complete your preparation log and one hand-checked order. Bring your workbook to Class 3, where we compare segments using Sales, Profit and average order value.
